Finished intelligence products are not press releases. They carry confidence levels, sourcing caveats, dissenting analyst views, and collection method fingerprints. Foreign intelligence services do not read declassified documents the same way American voters do. They read them as technical documents. They look for what was collected, when, through what methods, and at what resolution. A finished product that reveals an operation in granular detail tells Moscow or Tehran something about where U.S. collection was strong. A product that is vague about a known operation tells them where it was weak. Gabbard's release, whatever its domestic political purpose, is now a targeting document for every foreign service trying to map U.S. intelligence gaps around the 2020 cycle.
